messages.author: 2ae2b9a356853ad1
messages.subject: CODEX for targeted sequencing
parts:
Hello,

Veronique Geoffroy and I are two french users very interested in the CODEX R package. We are currently working on targeted exome data and not WES, and we try to implement the CODEX package with our particular data separating chromosome by chromosome. It seems to work for the moment, but we would be very happy if a version for exon targeted appears !

We would like to keep connected to the codex google group, so that we keep aware of any evolution or new release : do we need any inscription or just mail this mailing is ok ?
If a new release is being undertaken, do we already now approximately when it is going to be available ?

Thank you all for the answers !

Yvan Herenger
Interne DES Génétique Médicale
Master 2 Biologie des Structures et Bioinformatique

messages.author: 94ec915e8ce36448
messages.subject: Re: joining the codex group
parts:
Hello Yvan,

Our targeted sequencing designs have both exons and full genes captured. This varies and depends on your experimental (capture array) design. I think from your .bed file yours capture the full genes and some genes can be very long, up to 500 kb. CODEX (and I think other methods too) won’t recover CNV signals from this large a region, especially if only partial gene undergoes CNV event. Furthermore, our experience shows that exonic and intronic regions have bait biases in targeted sequencing (again, this is in our design and this varies between different dataset). What we did is we binned the genes that were captured as full into the exons they contain and thus kept only the reads mapped to exons and threw away intronic reads.

Hope this clarifies,
Yuchao

parts:
Exactly, some of our targets are much bigger than the size threshold. And in fact, as our design encompasses really few genes, our depth of coverage also is much bigger than the depth threshold.
To make CODEX suit our data, I devided the genes targets into exon and intron to get the required number of targets and decrease their sizes. I also changed the thresholds in the code : that way we complete the analysis but we I do not find the known anomalies.

I wonder if I should better not change the threshold - that are already expected to be optimal - and better try to make our data suit CODEX than the opposite ?
Did you change something in the algorithm and the R function to make CODEX run on targeted exome ?
And if you did, may I dare ask you to try the new code on my data ?

Yvan

messages.subject: Re: joining the codex group
parts:
Hi Yuchao,

Many thanks for your mail !
I hope everything went good for your midterm and the paper ?

Actually, I was going to write you today about my new results and questions about CODEX.

Well, briefly, I did again the analysis from the beginning following your advices : I prepared the .bed files the better I could using only the exons of each genes (and avoiding gene long targets) to avoid biases due to intronic capture, I used the default parameters (expected to be optimal) and I payed attention about everything we told about before and every advices you gave me. I am still working with version 0.99.4.
In a set of 7 CNV I of exonic size, I detect very well one CNV (a homozygous deletion), I have several false positives that I can explain me and false negatives that I cannot explain sometimes. Sometimes, when expecting to find something I get after the "choiceofK" step :
> choiceofK(AIC, BIC, RSS, K, filename = paste(projectname, "_", chr, "_choiceofK", ".pdf", sep = ""))
null device
1

My question are :
I join you 2 .txt of a false negative result and a false positive result to show you better my problem with my remarques and questions inside at the end of the file : can you have a look once you'll have time enough for that ? Is it a matter of threshold ?
Is this "null device" an error message explaining why I don't find the expected result ?

Besides that, really thank you for the codes : I will try it very soon, as well as I will update to the 0.99.10 version. I'll let you know about that soon !

Cheers,

Yvan

parts:
Hi Yvan,

Just a few suggestions from my side—see below.

1) Please update your CODEX to 0.99.10.
2) Please use the code that I sent you last week to process the entire chromosome altogether (essentially the code extracts read depth, GC content etc from each chromosome separately but does the normalization at one attempt). From the log files you sent me, I believe you ran chr11 and chr12 themselves? This way you only have 24 and 63 targets respectively after QC, which reduces CODEX’s power.
3) For your false positive and false negative, usually it’s very hard to define these unless you have gold standard, e.g., paired SNP array calls or array CGH calls. I don’t usually refer to the raw depth coverage matrix (aka, Y matrix) for CNV signals since the data can be noisy and it’s hard to distinguish a CNV signal from artifacts/biases. Nevertheless, targeted sequencing tends to be cleaner than WES and therefore I think your intuition is right. What’s the chosen K by CODEX for your dataset (K=which.max(BIC) by default but the choice of K is not trivial)? I would suggest K=1.
4) Finally, do you have case and control samples? If so, please use normalize2() for normalization rather than normalize(). This increases calling accuracy.
5) The ’null device’ is from the plotting command — a pdf is generated from your Linux device rather than your “local” device. This isn’t an error.

Let me know if you’ve any questions and please keep me updated on how the new code works on your data! Thanks.

Best regards,
Yuchao

parts:
Hi Jens,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. There are two versions for CODEX. The one we described in our paper and we included in the Bioconductor paper is for whole exome sequencing. It normalizes and segments each chromosome separately. You can combine all chromosomes together for normalization but it's very computationally heavy (n=200,000 exons). For segmentation, naturally and by default we detect CNVs by segmenting each chromosome separately.

We adapt CODEX for targeted sequencing due to general interest. The number of targets are too few if we consider chromosomes separately and thus we normalize all genome-wide targets altogether. For segmentation, we do that on the gene - level as between different genes(targets) the distance can be quite large. So we perform segmentation within each gene.

Hope that this clarifies. Let us know if you have any further questions.

Cheers,
Yuchao

Hi Yvan,

Just a few suggestions from my side—see below.

1) Please update your CODEX to 0.99.10.
2) Please use the code that I sent you last week to process the entire chromosome altogether (essentially the code extracts read depth, GC content etc from each chromosome separately but does the normalization at one attempt). From the log files you sent me, I believe you ran chr11 and chr12 themselves? This way you only have 24 and 63 targets respectively after QC, which reduces CODEX’s power.
3) For your false positive and false negative, usually it’s very hard to define these unless you have gold standard, e.g., paired SNP array calls or array CGH calls. I don’t usually refer to the raw depth coverage matrix (aka, Y matrix) for CNV signals since the data can be noisy and it’s hard to distinguish a CNV signal from artifacts/biases. Nevertheless, targeted sequencing tends to be cleaner than WES and therefore I think your intuition is right. What’s the chosen K by CODEX for your dataset (K=which.max(BIC) by default but the choice of K is not trivial)? I would suggest K=1.
4) Finally, do you have case and control samples? If so, please use normalize2() for normalization rather than normalize(). This increases calling accuracy.
5) The ’null device’ is from the plotting command — a pdf is generated from your Linux device rather than your “local” device. This isn’t an error.

Let me know if you’ve any questions and please keep me updated on how the new code works on your data! Thanks.
